# Purpose and Motivation of RLHF

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is used to better align AI model behavior with human values and preferences. Traditional supervised training of large models (e.g. next-word prediction on internet text) often yields models that **are not reliably tuned to what humans actually want** – they might produce correct but unhelpful or unsafe answers. RLHF addresses this gap by incorporating human feedback into the training loop, effectively using human judgments as an additional optimization signal. This is significant for **AI alignment** because many tasks have goals that are _“complex, poorly-defined, or hard to specify”_, leading to a mismatch between what we truly want and what a naive objective would optimize ([Using reinforcement learning from human feedback to fine-tune large language models](https://labelbox.com/blog/using-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback-to-fine-tune-large-language-models/#:~:text=As%20stated%20in%20,%E2%80%9D)). By having humans directly evaluate or compare model outputs, RLHF allows the training process to capture nuances of human values that are difficult to encode in a traditional reward function. In practice, RLHF has been shown to markedly improve model behavior _beyond_ what supervised learning alone can achieve. For example, a GPT-3 model fine-tuned with RLHF (InstructGPT) was **strongly preferred** by human labelers over the original GPT-3, showing higher helpfulness and accuracy and reduced harmful outputs ([Using reinforcement learning from human feedback to fine-tune large language models](https://labelbox.com/blog/using-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback-to-fine-tune-large-language-models/#:~:text=RLHF%20is%20a%20powerful%20tool,to%20achieve%20a%20variety%20of)). Studies from OpenAI and Anthropic found that _“RLHF improves helpfulness and harmlessness by a huge margin”_ compared to only scaling up models ([Using reinforcement learning from human feedback to fine-tune large language models](https://labelbox.com/blog/using-reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback-to-fine-tune-large-language-models/#:~:text=InstructGPT%20%28a%20model%20fine,to%20achieve%20a%20variety%20of)). In summary, the purpose of RLHF is to **fine-tune AI systems to be more useful, safer, and aligned** with human intentions than is possible with supervised learning alone, using human feedback as a guide to what _“good”_ behavior looks like.

# General Working Mechanism of RLHF

RLHF augments the standard training of a model with an additional feedback loop based on human preferences. The overall process typically involves multiple stages:

1. **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**: Start with a pretrained model and fine-tune it on a small set of **human-written demonstration data**. For example, human labelers provide example prompts and high-quality responses, and the model is trained to mimic these responses. This supervised policy (the SFT model) establishes a reasonable initial behavior for the model ([How ChatGPT actually works](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/how-chatgpt-actually-works/#:~:text=Fine,of%20three%20distinct%20steps)).
    
2. **Collecting Human Preference Data**: Using the SFT model, generate many candidate outputs for various prompts. Humans are then asked to **rank or choose the best output** among these candidates. This yields a dataset of comparisons (for each prompt, some outputs are labeled as more preferred than others) ([How ChatGPT actually works](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/how-chatgpt-actually-works/#:~:text=supervised%20policy%20,called%20policy%20model)). These human preferences serve as the ground truth for what constitutes a better vs. worse answer.
    
3. **Reward Model Training**: Train a **reward model** (often a neural network initialized from the same base model) to predict human preferences. The reward model $r_\phi(x,y)$ takes a prompt $x$ and a candidate output $y$ and outputs a scalar _reward_ score that should be **higher for human-preferred outputs**. Training $r_\phi$ is done using the comparison data: the model is optimized so that for each pair $(y_w, y_l)$ (winner vs. loser) it assigns a higher score to $y_w$ than to $y_l$. A typical loss function is derived from the Bradley-Terry model or a binary logistic regression setup ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=of%20preferences%20%24x%2C%20y_,preferences%20by%20minimizing%20the%20loss)) ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Ctag%7B3%7D%20%5Clabel%7Beq%3Areward,right)). Concretely, if we have a winning response $y_w$ and losing response $y_l$ for the same prompt, we maximize $\log \sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w) - r_\phi(x,y_l))$ (or equivalently minimize the negative of that) so that the reward model learns to rank $y_w$ above $y_l$ ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Ctag%7B3%7D%20%5Clabel%7Beq%3Areward,right)). This training procedure yields a reward function that **mimics human judgments** on the quality of responses.
    
4. **Policy Optimization (RL Fine-Tuning)**: The final stage treats the language model (policy $\pi_\theta$) as an agent in a _single-step reinforcement learning_ setting. The model generates an output $y$ for a given prompt $x$ (this is the “action”), and it receives a reward equal to the reward model’s score $r_\phi(x,y)$. Using reinforcement learning algorithms, we then **fine-tune the policy to maximize the expected reward**. In other words, we adjust the model’s parameters so that it preferentially produces answers that the reward model (and hence humans) would rate highly ([RLHF and DPO Compared - CROWDWORKS Blog](https://crowdworks.blog/en/rlhf-and-dpo-compared/#:~:text=The%20reward%20model%20in%20RLHF,modular%20system%20outputting%20a%20reward)) ([RLHF and DPO Compared - CROWDWORKS Blog](https://crowdworks.blog/en/rlhf-and-dpo-compared/#:~:text=training%20minimizes%20errors%20concerning%20correct,to%20optimize%20that%20objective%20function)). This step often uses an _on-policy_ RL algorithm: the current policy is used to sample outputs for a batch of prompts, those outputs are scored by the reward model, and the policy is updated to increase the probability of high-reward outputs and decrease the probability of low-reward ones.
    

A popular choice for this RL step is **Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)**, which is a stable policy-gradient method well-suited for large models. PPO incrementally adjusts the model, treating the reward model as a **learnable loss function** that reflects human preferences ([RLHF and DPO Compared - CROWDWORKS Blog](https://crowdworks.blog/en/rlhf-and-dpo-compared/#:~:text=Reinforcement%20Learning%20,to%20optimize%20that%20objective%20function)). In practice, an **additional caution** is added during policy optimization to avoid the model drifting too far from its original fluent behavior. Specifically, the objective typically includes a Kullback-Leibler **(KL) penalty** between the new policy $\pi_\theta$ and the original model (often the SFT policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$). This means the RL update not only seeks to maximize the reward model’s score but also **penalizes large deviations** from the reference policy ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=Minimizing%20deviation%3A%20The%20term%20,producing%20bizarre%20or%20unexpected%20responses)). Intuitively, this keeps the model’s outputs reasonable and prevents it from exploiting quirks of the reward model (“going off distribution”). The result of RLHF is a fine-tuned policy that produces answers maximizing a balance of **human-preference reward and fidelity to the original model’s distribution** ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=Minimizing%20deviation%3A%20The%20term%20,producing%20bizarre%20or%20unexpected%20responses)). In deployment (e.g. ChatGPT), this final fine-tuned model can respond to user inputs in ways that are more helpful, correct, and aligned with user intentions than the original model.

# Mathematical Formulation of RLHF

Mathematically, RLHF can be framed as an **optimization problem** involving two coupled objectives: one for the reward model and one for the policy. The _reward modeling_ step can be seen as an inference or _inverse learning_ problem, while the _policy optimization_ step is a direct reinforcement learning problem. Formally:

- **Reward Model Objective**: The reward model $r_\phi(x,y)$ is trained to approximate human preference judgments. Given a dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of human comparisons, we optimize $\phi$ to **maximize the likelihood of the human-preferred outcomes**. For example, for a pair $(y_w, y_l)$ (preferred “win” vs. less preferred “lose”) for prompt $x$, we can use a binary cross-entropy or pairwise logistic loss:
    
    $L_{reward}(ϕ)  =  −E_{(x, yw, yl)∼D}[log ⁡ σ ⁣(r_ϕ(x,y_w)−r_ϕ(x,y_l))]$
    
    where $\sigma$ is the sigmoid function ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Ctag%7B3%7D%20%5Clabel%7Beq%3Areward,right)). Minimizing this loss pushes $r_\phi(x,y_w)$ higher than $r_\phi(x,y_l)$ for each comparison, aligning the reward function with human preference orderings. This formulation uses only **differences of rewards**, so any constant offset in $r_\phi$ doesn’t matter; the model focuses on getting the relative ordering right ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Ctag%7B3%7D%20%5Clabel%7Beq%3Areward,right)). Solving this to optimality would yield a reward function that, for any new prompt and pair of candidate answers, can predict which answer humans would prefer.
    
- **Policy Optimization Objective**: We treat the language model $\pi_\theta(y|x)$ as a policy that we want to adjust to maximize the expected reward from $r_\phi$. In a simple form, the objective for the policy is:
    
    $$J(θ)  =  E_{x∼D_{prompt}}[ Ey∼πθ(⋅∣x)[ rϕ(x,y) ]] ,$$
    
    meaning we want to maximize the expected reward $r_\phi(x,y)$ when $y$ is drawn from the policy for prompt $x$. In practice, a **constraint or penalty** is included to prevent $\pi_\theta$ from straying too far from the initial policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (often the SFT model). This is often implemented via a KL-divergence regularization: for example, the _augmented_ objective can be written as
    
    $$J_{KL}(θ)  =  Ex,y[rϕ(x,y)]  −  β Ex[DKL(πθ(⋅∣x) ∥ πref(⋅∣x))]$$
    
    where $\beta$ is a coefficient controlling the strength of the penalty ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=Minimizing%20deviation%3A%20The%20term%20,producing%20bizarre%20or%20unexpected%20responses)). This term $D_{\text{KL}}$ discourages the policy from devoting too much probability mass to sequences that the reference model would consider unlikely (thereby keeping outputs _reasonable_ and preventing reward hacking). Equivalently, one can view this regularized objective as maximizing $ \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[r_\phi(x,y) - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}]$ ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=Minimizing%20deviation%3A%20The%20term%20,producing%20bizarre%20or%20unexpected%20responses)). Solving this constrained optimization yields a **balanced policy** that tries to be high-reward but not too deviant from the original model.
    

Notably, the **optimal solution** to the above regularized objective has an analytic form: it can be shown (via calculus of variations or the principle of maximum entropy) that the _optimal_ policy satisfying $r_\phi$ maximization and a KL constraint is

$$π^∗(y∣x)  ∝  π_{ref}(y∣x) exp⁡ ⁣(\frac{1}{β} r_ϕ(x,y))$$

i.e. $\pi^*(y|x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)},\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta}r_\phi(x,y))$ for some normalizing $Z(x)$ ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Cpi_r%28y%20%5Cmid%20x%29%20%3D%20%5Cfrac,beta%7D%20r%28x%2C%20y%29%20%5Cright)). This _Boltzmann policy_ form shows that the new policy should reweight the reference policy by an exponential factor favoring high-reward outputs ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Cpi_r%28y%20%5Cmid%20x%29%20%3D%20%5Cfrac,beta%7D%20r%28x%2C%20y%29%20%5Cright)). The KL penalty parameter $\beta$ acts like a temperature controlling how strongly the policy concentrates on reward versus staying close to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. In practice, we don’t directly compute this formula (because $r_\phi$ is learned and $Z(x)$ is intractable), but RL algorithms aim to approximate this optimal policy.

**Training RLHF as an EM-like process:** We can interpret RLHF training as an **iterative two-step procedure** analogous to _expectation-maximization_. First, given the current policy’s behavior, we perform a form of _inverse reinforcement learning_ by training the reward model to match human preferences (estimating the “latent” reward function that explains why humans prefer certain outputs). This is akin to an **E-step** where we infer reward values for outputs. Next, keeping that reward function fixed, we perform a _policy improvement_ step – adjusting the policy to maximize the expected reward (approximately following the analytic solution above) – analogous to an **M-step** where we maximize the expected reward objective. In practice, RLHF may alternate these steps or perform them sequentially (often one round of reward model training followed by one round of policy RL fine-tuning). This alternating view highlights that RLHF is **aligning the model to human preferences** by continually refining the reward estimate and then _pushing the model to optimize it_. The result is a closed loop where human feedback (through the reward model) directs the policy update, and the policy’s new outputs, in turn, require the reward model to remain accurate – ensuring the system remains grounded in human-defined notions of quality.

# PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) in RLHF

**Intuition and Role of PPO:** Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that has become a standard choice for RLHF fine-tuning (used in OpenAI’s InstructGPT and ChatGPT training). The intuition behind PPO is to allow the policy to improve (increase reward) while **keeping updates stable and “close” to the previous policy**. In the context of RLHF, this is crucial: we want to gradually nudge a language model to better align with preferences without destroying the valuable knowledge it acquired during pre-training or making its behavior erratic. PPO is essentially a refined policy gradient method that avoids large swings in the policy by limiting how much the new policy can depart from the old policy in a single update ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=PPO%20is%20motivated%20by%20the,least%20as%20well%20as%20TRPO)) ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=PPO,far%20from%20the%20old%20policy)). This aligns perfectly with RLHF’s needs, where maintaining fluency and coherence (close to the reference model) is important even as we optimize for higher reward. PPO’s popularity in RLHF stems from its **simplicity and empirical effectiveness** – it doesn’t require complicated second-order optimization or value function tuning like some older algorithms, yet it achieves strong, stable improvements ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=PPO%20is%20motivated%20by%20the,to%20implement%2C%20and%20empirically%20seem)).

**Clipped Surrogate Objective and Policy Stability:** PPO introduces a _clipped surrogate objective_ to restrain policy updates. In each iteration, PPO computes the probability ratio between the new policy $\pi_\theta$ and the old policy $\pi_{\text{old}}$ for the actions taken. For a given prompt $x$ and an output $y$, this ratio is $r(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(y|x)}$. A naive policy gradient would encourage $r(\theta)$ to become large if $y$ had high advantage (meaning $y$ received a high reward relative to expectation) – i.e., drastically increasing $\pi_\theta(y|x)$. PPO instead uses the clipped objective:

$$L(θ)=E_{x,y∼π_{old}}​​[min(r(θ)A^{π_{old}}​(x,y),clip(r(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^{π_{old}}​(x,y))],$$

where $A^{\pi_{\text{old}}}(x,y)$ is the advantage (how much better $y$ was than average for that prompt) and $\epsilon$ is a small threshold (e.g. 0.1 or 0.2). This objective essentially says:

> “If an action/output $y$ is advantageous, you can increase its probability, but **only up to** $(1+\epsilon)$ times the old probability; if an output is disadvantageous, you can decrease its probability, but not below $(1-\epsilon)$ times the old probability.” ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Because%20the%20advantage%20is%20positive%2C,away%20from%20the%20old%20policy)) ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Image%3A%20L%28s%2Ca%2C%5Ctheta_k%2C%5Ctheta%29%20%3D%20%5Cmax%5Cleft%28%20%5Cfrac,%5Cepsilon%29%20%5Cright%29%20A%5E%7B%5Cpi_%7B%5Ctheta_k%7D%7D%28s%2Ca))

Any further increase or decrease beyond that yields no additional gain in the objective (the $\min$ truncates the benefit) ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Because%20the%20advantage%20is%20positive%2C,away%20from%20the%20old%20policy)) ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Image%3A%20L%28s%2Ca%2C%5Ctheta_k%2C%5Ctheta%29%20%3D%20%5Cmax%5Cleft%28%20%5Cfrac,%5Cepsilon%29%20%5Cright%29%20A%5E%7B%5Cpi_%7B%5Ctheta_k%7D%7D%28s%2Ca)). This clever clipping mechanism prevents any single update from **pushing the policy too far**, avoiding instability. It improves policy stability by ensuring the new policy stays within a “trust region” of the old one, but without the complexity of a hard constraint. In effect, PPO **penalizes extreme policy changes** implicitly: once the policy tries to move beyond the $\epsilon$ range in either direction for a given action, the objective flattens out, removing the incentive to move further ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=becomes%20more%20likely%E2%80%94that%20is%2C%20if,away%20from%20the%20old%20policy)) ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Advantage%20is%20negative%3A%20Suppose%20the,to%20the%20objective%20reduces%20to)). This yields more reliable and robust training, which is particularly important for language models where an out-of-distribution shift can degrade performance.

**Key PPO Equations:** The core of PPO can be summarized by the **surrogate objective** above. For completeness, the probability ratio is $r(\theta)=\pi_\theta(y|x)/\pi_{\text{old}}(y|x)$ and the _clipped_ version is $\tilde{r}(\theta) = \text{clip}(r(\theta),,1-\epsilon,,1+\epsilon)$. PPO then maximizes the expectation of $\min(r(\theta)A, \tilde{r}(\theta)A)$ ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Image%3A%20L%28s%2Ca%2C%5Ctheta_k%2C%5Ctheta%29%20%3D%20%5Cmin%5Cleft%28%20%5Cfrac,pi_%7B%5Ctheta_k%7D%7D%28s%2Ca%29%20%5Cright)). In practice, $A^{\pi_{\text{old}}}(x,y)$ (the advantage) can be just the reward minus a baseline, since in one-step tasks the _advantage_ is simply the reward minus some reference (often they subtract a baseline equal to the reward model’s predicted value or the mean reward to reduce variance). The update rule can be seen as performing (stochastic) gradient ascent on this objective. A simplified view is:

- If $A$ is positive (the output $y$ was better than baseline), we want to increase $\pi_\theta(y|x)$ (i.e. $r(\theta)$ > 1 improves the objective), but gains cap out once $\pi_\theta$ is $(1+\epsilon)$ times the old policy ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=Because%20the%20advantage%20is%20positive%2C,away%20from%20the%20old%20policy)).
- If $A$ is negative, we want to decrease $\pi_\theta(y|x)$ (drive $r(\theta)$ below 1), but beyond a $(1-\epsilon)$ fractional decrease, further lowering is not beneficial ([Proximal Policy Optimization — Spinning Up documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html#:~:text=negative%2C%20in%20which%20case%20its,to%20the%20objective%20reduces%20to)).

This can be contrasted with a naive policy gradient which would lack such a cap and could push probabilities too high or too low in one step. Mathematically, PPO’s **update** can be written as finding $\theta_{new}$ that approximately maximizes:

$$L_{clip}​(θ)=E_{x,y∼π_{old}}​​[min \{{r(θ)A,clip(r(θ),1±ϵ)A\}}],$$

with the understanding that clip$(r,1\pm\epsilon)$ equals $\max(\min(r,1+\epsilon),,1-\epsilon)$ . Additional terms often used in PPO implementations include an **entropy bonus** (to keep the policy output distribution sufficiently random and prevent early collapse) and sometimes an explicit KL penalty (monitoring $D_{\text{KL}}$ between new and old policies, to stop training if it exceeds a threshold). Overall, PPO provides a convenient balance of **performance and safety** for RLHF: it lets the model significantly improve along the reward dimension while maintaining stable training dynamics and keeping the model’s behavior close to the reference point.

# DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)

**What is DPO and Why Different from PPO:** Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a newer technique that fundamentally rethinks the RLHF procedure. Whereas PPO-based RLHF uses an **explicit reward model and a reinforcement learning loop**, DPO aims to _collapse the problem into a single, direct optimization step_ on human preference data. 

The key difference is that **DPO removes the need for a separate reward model and avoids the RL training altogether** – it directly optimizes the policy using the _comparative feedback data_ (the same data used to train the reward model in RLHF). In essence, DPO treats alignment as a **supervised learning problem on comparisons**, rather than a reinforcement learning problem ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=The%20direct%20preference%20optimization%20,in%20a%20number%20of%20experiments)) ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=without%20having%20to%20sample%20from,in%20a%20number%20of%20experiments)). This is possible because, as theory shows, standard RLHF (with an optimal reward model and a KL constraint) has a specific optimum that one can solve for in closed form ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=1,of%20the%20Policy)). DPO leverages that insight to directly adjust the policy _as if we had done RLHF_, but via a simpler loss function.

**Eliminating the Reward Model (Preference-Based Loss):** In DPO, we assume we have a _reference policy_ $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ (e.g. the SFT model distribution) and a new policy $\pi_\theta$ we want to train. Rather than training $r_\phi$ explicitly, DPO derives a loss for $\pi_\theta$ such that **maximizing this loss causes $\pi_\theta$ to implicitly incorporate human preference information**. Starting from the optimal RLHF condition $\pi^*(y|x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\exp(\frac{1}{\beta}r(x,y))$, the DPO derivation shows that one can express differences in reward purely in terms of ratios of $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=express%20the%20reward%20as%20a,function%20of%20the%20optimal%20policy)) ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=The%20reward%20%24r_,learned%20by%20minimizing%20the%20loss)). The result is a **direct loss function on the policy**:

$L_{DPO}​(θ)=−E(x,yw​,yl​)∼D​[logσ(βlogπref​(yw​∣x)πθ​(yw​∣x)​−βlogπref​(yl​∣x)πθ​(yl​∣x)​)],$

where $y_w$ is the human-preferred output and $y_l$ the less preferred output for prompt $x$ ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=%5C%5B%5Cmathcal%7BL%7D_%7B%5Ctext%7BDPO%7D%7D%28%5Cpi_%5Ctheta%20%3B%20%5Cpi_%7B%5Ctext%7Bref%7D%7D%29%20%3A%3D%20,ref%7D%7D%28y_l%20%5Cmid%20x%29%7D%20%5Cright%29%20%5Cright)). This looks similar to the reward model loss earlier, but notice that **$r_\phi(x,\cdot)$ has disappeared** – instead, the _policy’s own logits_ (relative to the reference policy) serve in its place. Intuitively, DPO is saying: _“Adjust $\pi_\theta$ so that, for each comparison, the probability of the preferred answer is higher than the probability of the dispreferred answer – up to a factor determined by $\beta$.”_ It is effectively **pushing $\pi_\theta$ toward the optimal $\pi^*$ directly** by using the preference data as constraints on $\pi_\theta$. By optimizing this loss (e.g. via gradient descent, which is similar to standard supervised learning), the policy $\pi_\theta$ is directly trained to **satisfy the human preferences**. Crucially, this means we no longer need to train a reward model or perform iterative PPO updates with sampled trajectories; we can use the static dataset of comparisons to drive the policy update.

**Theoretical Advantages of DPO:** DPO offers several appealing advantages:

- _Simplicity:_ The training reduces to a **single-stage optimization** with a binary cross-entropy loss ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=need%20to%20set%20up%20a,can%20be%20tedious%20and%20overwhelming)) ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=Instead%2C%20DPO%20uses%20a%20binary,simplifies%20the%20whole%20development%20process)). This is much simpler to implement and tune compared to a full RL pipeline. There’s no need to manage separate reward model training epochs, PPO epochs, advantage estimation, or carefully tuned KL penalties – DPO has **no explicit “RL” hyperparameters**, since it’s effectively supervised learning on pairs.
- _Stability:_ By avoiding the reinforcement learning loop (which can be unstable and sensitive to hyperparameters), DPO tends to be very stable. Researchers note that DPO fine-tuning is _“stable, performant, and computationally lightweight”_, eliminating the need for extensive sampling or delicate hyperparameter tuning ([[2305.18290] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290#:~:text=estimated%20reward%20without%20drifting%20too,tuning)) ([[2305.18290] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290#:~:text=resulting%20algorithm%2C%20which%20we%20call,simpler%20to%20implement%20and%20train)). In large-scale experiments, DPO training has been shown to scale well (even up to 70B-parameter models) without the instabilities that can plague RL training ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=,Bench%20leaderboard)). For instance, one open benchmark found that a 70B model fine-tuned with DPO was not only stable but achieved **state-of-the-art alignment results**, outperforming even some larger RLHF-trained models ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=,Bench%20leaderboard)).
- _Efficiency:_ DPO is more computationally efficient because it doesn’t require on-policy sampling of new outputs at each step. In RLHF/PPO, each policy update typically requires generating many samples with the current policy to estimate gradients, and the reward model must be queried for each. DPO can use a fixed corpus of (prompt, comparison) samples and train with standard minibatch updates, much like a normal classifier. This **offline training** approach can be faster and use data more effectively. Moreover, by cutting out the reward model, we reduce the number of forward passes and memory overhead during training. Overall, DPO often requires less compute to reach similar performance ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=need%20to%20set%20up%20a,can%20be%20tedious%20and%20overwhelming)) ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=Instead%2C%20DPO%20uses%20a%20binary,simplifies%20the%20whole%20development%20process)).
- _No Reward Model Exploitation:_* An important subtle benefit is that DPO avoids the phenomenon of **reward model hacking**. In RLHF, the policy might learn to game the learned reward model (finding loopholes to get a high score that don’t actually correspond to truly better outputs – a form of “wireheading”). DPO sidesteps this because there is no separate reward network to game; the training signal comes directly from human comparisons. One can think that DPO directly optimizes the _pairwise preference likelihood_, which is exactly aligned with what we want, whereas RLHF optimizes a proxy (the reward model) that can be imperfect. In theory, if the preference data is good, DPO will converge to a policy that maximizes the same underlying objective as RLHF _without giving the model opportunities to exploit an imperfect reward function_ ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=without%20having%20to%20sample%20from,in%20a%20number%20of%20experiments)). (The DPO loss derives from the same objective as RLHF’s reward maximization, so it’s not optimizing something different – it’s just a different route to the same optimum ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=The%20direct%20preference%20optimization%20,in%20a%20number%20of%20experiments)).)

In summary, DPO reframes the human feedback optimization as a direct supervised learning problem on comparisons. By doing so, it **removes the need for an explicit reward model and an RL control loop**, achieving a simpler and often more robust pipeline for alignment. The policy is trained via a straightforward classification-style loss that says “make the preferred output more likely than the dispreferred one, relative to the base model,” which naturally incorporates both the preference and the notion of staying near the base distribution (since $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ appears in the loss as a baseline). This built-in reference term plays a similar role to the KL penalty in PPO, so DPO inherently keeps the policy from straying too far while improving alignment.

**Mathematical Formulation of DPO:** From the earlier equation, we can see the DPO objective more clearly by simplifying the expression inside the sigmoid:

βlog⁡πθ(yw∣x)πref(yw∣x)  −  βlog⁡πθ(yl∣x)πref(yl∣x)  =  β[log⁡πθ(yw∣x)−log⁡πθ(yl∣x)]  −  β[log⁡πref(yw∣x)−log⁡πref(yl∣x)] .\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)} \;-\; \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)} \;=\; \beta \Big[\log \pi_\theta(y_w|x) - \log \pi_\theta(y_l|x)\Big]\;-\;\beta\Big[\log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x) - \log \pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)\Big]\,.

This is essentially $\beta [\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w|x)}{\pi_\theta(y_l|x)} - \log \frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l|x)}]$. The sigmoid $\sigma(z)$ then represents the model’s predicted probability that $y_w$ is preferred over $y_l$. So $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}$ is a logistic loss that encourages that probability to be close to 1 for the human-labeled preferred pair. This objective is optimized with respect to $\pi_\theta$’s parameters (with $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ fixed and acting as a constant in the loss). In practice, one picks a value of $\beta$ (analogous to the inverse temperature; it can be tuned or set to 1 for simplicity) and then just **trains the new policy network on all the comparison samples** using the above loss. This direct optimization has been empirically shown to achieve results on par with or better than PPO-based RLHF on several tasks ([[2305.18290] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290#:~:text=resulting%20algorithm%2C%20which%20we%20call,simpler%20to%20implement%20and%20train)) ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=Image)), confirming the theoretical equivalence in objective.

# Comparison of PPO and DPO

Both PPO-based RLHF and Direct Preference Optimization aim to produce models aligned with human preferences, but they differ in methodology and have distinct trade-offs:

- **Training Procedure**: _PPO-based RLHF_ is a two-phase approach (learn reward model, then do on-policy RL updates), whereas _DPO_ is a one-phase direct fine-tuning using preference data. PPO requires a **reward model** to provide a reward signal and an RL algorithm to improve the policy; DPO **bypasses the reward model**, using the preference data directly as the training signal ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=need%20to%20set%20up%20a,can%20be%20tedious%20and%20overwhelming)). This makes DPO’s implementation much simpler, avoiding the need for a delicate RL loop.
    
- **Stability and Robustness**: PPO RLHF can be **unstable** if not carefully tuned – the interplay of reward model quality, learning rate, KL penalty, etc., can lead to policy collapse or reward hacking (e.g. the model finding degenerate ways to get a high reward score) ([How ChatGPT actually works](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/how-chatgpt-actually-works/#:~:text=Wireheading,away%20from%20some%20reference%20input)) ([What is direct preference optimization (DPO)? | SuperAnnotate](https://www.superannotate.com/blog/direct-preference-optimization-dpo#:~:text=The%20problem%20with%20RLHF)). DPO tends to be **more stable** by construction; it optimizes a convex (in terms of probabilities) cross-entropy loss, which generally has well-behaved convergence. In practice, DPO has shown strong stability even for very large models (tens of billions of parameters) ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=all%20other%20models%20on%20the,Bench%20leaderboard)), whereas PPO sometimes requires careful monitoring of KL-divergence to prevent divergence.
    
- **Efficiency**: PPO is an _on-policy algorithm_, meaning after each policy update, new samples must be drawn from the updated model to compute fresh gradients. This can be **computationally intensive**, as it requires generating a lot of text and evaluating it with the reward model at every iteration. DPO can work _off-policy_ with a fixed set of human preference comparisons, which is typically **more sample-efficient**. DPO’s training loop is similar to standard supervised fine-tuning – you can reuse the same comparisons for many epochs, and you don’t repeatedly query the model for new samples during training. This often translates to **faster training and lower cost** for DPO, given the same data. Additionally, maintaining a reward model in PPO RLHF adds overhead (both memory and computation for inference); DPO removes that overhead.
    
- **Objective and Theoretical Convergence**: Both approaches are theoretically trying to optimize a similar underlying objective (maximize human-preference alignment while keeping the language model plausible). PPO does so _implicitly_ via reward maximization plus regularization, whereas DPO does so _explicitly_ in a single loss function. In fact, DPO’s derivation shows it is optimizing the **same optimality condition** as RLHF’s reward-maximizing policy ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=without%20having%20to%20sample%20from,in%20a%20number%20of%20experiments)) ([RLHF without RL - Direct Preference Optimization | ICLR Blogposts 2024](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2024/blog/rlhf-without-rl/#:~:text=Thus%2C%20instead%20of%20first%20learning,perform%20rejection%20sampling)). Thus, in the limit of infinite data and ideal optimization, both PPO-RLHF and DPO should converge to the same optimal policy. In practice, PPO might reach a slightly different solution if the reward model is imperfect or if the KL penalty is not ideal, whereas DPO directly uses the data and might be less prone to such mismatches.
    
- **Hyperparameter Sensitivity**: PPO-based RLHF involves multiple hyperparameters – learning rate for the policy, reward model training settings, the KL penalty coefficient (or a schedule), advantage estimation parameters, etc. Tuning these can be complex, and suboptimal settings can either hinder learning or cause the model to diverge. DPO has fewer dials to turn. Its main hyperparameters are the reference policy (which is usually given) and the scalar $\beta$ (which controls how strongly preferences are enforced, analogous to the KL coefficient). Practitioners have found DPO requires **minimal hyperparameter tuning** to work out-of-the-box ([[2305.18290] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290#:~:text=resulting%20algorithm%2C%20which%20we%20call,simpler%20to%20implement%20and%20train)), making it attractive for rapid development.
    
- **Practical Usage and Maturity**: PPO-based RLHF has been **battle-tested** in real deployments (it’s how the original ChatGPT was trained) and there are established frameworks (such as TRLX, OpenAI Baselines, etc.) to apply it. DPO is _newer_ (proposed in 2023) and still being explored, but it has quickly gained traction. Libraries like Hugging Face’s TRL have incorporated DPO, and early results on various tasks (summarization, dialogue, controlling tone) show DPO performing **as well as or better than PPO-based training** ([[2305.18290] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290#:~:text=resulting%20algorithm%2C%20which%20we%20call,simpler%20to%20implement%20and%20train)). DPO’s simplicity makes it easy to try, but some in the community continue to use PPO for continuity and because it can integrate with other RL techniques (e.g. if one wanted to mix human reward with other reward terms or constraints, PPO provides a flexible framework).
    
- **When each is preferred**: In current practice, **RLHF with PPO** is used when one has a good reward model and possibly needs ongoing feedback integration (you can continually gather new human feedback and update the reward model and policy). It’s a natural choice if you treat the problem as an RL environment with humans in the loop. **DPO** is preferred when simplicity and stability are paramount, or when you have a fixed batch of preference data and want to avoid the complexity of RL. DPO is essentially _“RLHF without the RL”_, making it appealing for fine-tuning large models where one wants to minimize risk and computational overhead. One trade-off is that DPO, using a fixed dataset, doesn’t naturally incorporate _online learning_ from new feedback – whereas a PPO approach could be extended to an iterative loop that keeps improving with new human data. However, one can still iterate DPO in rounds (train a model, have humans label its outputs, then train further), so this is more of a workflow consideration than a fundamental limit.
    

In summary, **PPO vs DPO** in RLHF presents a trade-off between a more complex, reinforcement-learning-centric approach and a streamlined direct optimization approach. PPO has been the go-to for ensuring aligned behavior, offering fine-grained control at the cost of complexity, while DPO offers a lean alternative that leverages the same human preference information in a more direct way. In terms of **efficiency and ease**, DPO often wins (no reward model, less computation per update), and it has demonstrated strong results and stability. In terms of **proven track record and flexibility**, PPO is well-understood and has been successfully deployed at scale (with the KL regularization helping to guard against failure). As research in RLHF progresses, DPO’s rise suggests that many alignment tasks might not require full reinforcement learning treatment – instead, clever **preference optimization techniques** can achieve similar alignment with fewer moving parts. Nonetheless, both PPO and DPO remain valuable tools, and the choice may depend on the specific project needs: **if one prioritizes stability and simplicity, DPO is very attractive; if one needs a more traditional RL setup or already has an effective reward model in hand, PPO is a solid, if more involved, choice**.
